drift/file: Here is a short file that gives you GNU Hello from nix packages. It looks complete.
drift/angle: But look at the name in angle brackets. That name is not in the file. Nix looks it up on this machine.
drift/channel: It finds a channel: a copy of nix packages this machine last updated whenever somebody got round to it.
drift/two: So a laptop updated in March and a server updated in June read the same file, and build different things.
drift/want: What you want is a file that says exactly which nix packages it means.
shape/file: A flake is a folder with a file called flake dot nix. That file is an attribute set with three parts, and the first is a description.
shape/inputs: Inputs says what the flake depends on, by U R L. This one is a branch of nix packages on GitHub.
shape/outputs: Outputs is a function. Nix fetches every input and passes them in by name. Self is the flake itself.
shape/set: Legacy packages is where nix packages keeps its packages, one set per system. The odd name is only history.
shape/ret: The function returns an attribute set. A package goes under packages, then its system, then a name.
shape/known: That shape is the same in every flake, so tools know where to look. Nix build dot hash default builds exactly that attribute.
lock/first: A branch moves. So the first time you use a flake, Nix turns that branch into one exact commit, and writes it in flake dot lock.
lock/rev: Here is the pin. Rev is the exact commit.
lock/hash: N A R hash is a hash of what that commit contains, so a download that differs is rejected.
lock/commit: You commit this file to git, next to flake dot nix. Now everyone who checks out the repository evaluates against the same nix packages.
lock/moves: The branch keeps moving, and your builds stay exactly where they were.
lock/update: When you want newer packages, nix flake update moves the pin. It is a change you choose, and commit.
pure/err: Here is the classic surprise. In a git repository this fails, with flake dot nix sitting right there.
pure/tracked: A flake only sees files git tracks. A file git does not know about does not exist, as far as Nix is concerned.
pure/why: That is on purpose. A stray local file can never slip into a build nobody else can reproduce.
pure/build: Add the file and it builds. Dot hash default means the flake in this folder, and its output called default.
pure/run: A flake can live anywhere. Nix run, then a GitHub address fetches one, builds it and runs it.
pure/pure: Evaluation is pure as well. Inside a flake there is no nix packages in angle brackets, no current system, and environment variables read as empty.
pure/end: So what a flake builds depends only on its tracked files and its pinned inputs, and those are the same on every machine.
